name: Balanced
description: You are given a cyclic array $$$a$$$ with $$$n$$$ elements, where $$$n$$$ is odd . In each operation, you can do the following: Choose an index $$$1 \le i \le n$$$ and increase $$$a_{i - 1}$$$ by $$$1$$$, $$$a_i$$$ by $$$2$$$, and $$$a_{i + 1}$$$ by $$$1$$$. The element before the first element is the last element because this is a cyclic array. A cyclic array is called balanced if all its elements are equal to each other. Find any sequence of operations to make this cyclic array balanced or determine that it is impossible. Please note that you do not have to minimize the number of operations.
input_specification: Each test consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \lt 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$n$$$ is odd ) — the length of the array $$$a$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^{6}$$$) — the elements of the array $$$a$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case: If it is impossible to make the cyclic array balanced, output $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, output $$$n$$$ integers $$$v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n$$$ ($$$0 \leq v_i \leq 10^{18}$$$) — where $$$v_i$$$ denotes the number of operations applied to index $$$i$$$. It can be proved that if any solution exists, then there exists a solution under the given constraints. If there are several solutions under the given constraints, output any of them.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2032E — Balanced [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
